performers: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, baritone; Berlin Philharmonic; Rudolf Kempe, conductor
intro: “In diesem Wetter, in diesem Braus” is the fifth and last song of Kindertotenlieder: a father rages at the weather, then sings his children to sleep, and the storm music is followed by a lullaby with celesta. Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau sings with the Berlin Philharmonic under Rudolf Kempe.

sections.label: A · The father in the storm
sections.mNote: Winds, trembling cellos and sharp harp chords.

sections.label: Link · Piccolo and small bell
sections.mNote: The storm music slows over a held high note.

sections.label: B · Lullaby in D major
sections.mNote: Celesta and soft strings play a rocking figure beneath the baritone.

sections.label: Coda · Horns after the voice
sections.mNote: Bassoon and horns play above the rocking figure in the violas.

cues.title: Opening of the storm
cues.text: The winds play short phrases, the cellos tremble and the harp strikes accented chords. Much of the storm begins softly. Mahler marked the passage “ruhelos schmerzvollem Ausdruck” (restless, painful expression) before Fischer-Dieskau has sung a word.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460 (1905), p. 60: Mit ruhelos schmerzvollem Ausdruck and the opening dynamics; our translation. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Opening march in D minor
cues.text: The storm is set as a march in D minor. Its key and melodic style recall the first movement of Mahler’s Third Symphony, written in 1895–96. No other song in the cycle opens with a march.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, Universal Edition introduction to Kindertotenlieder (autumn 2008): song 5 “is the only song to open with a Mahler-style march”, recalling the key and melodic style of the Third Symphony’s first movement (song bar 9, symphony bar 136): https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027

cues.title: First stanza, Rückert’s text
cues.text: The father in Rückert’s poem says repeatedly that he would never have sent his children out in such weather. He then corrects himself: “man hat sie getragen hinaus” — they were carried out. “Ich durfte nichts dazu sagen” — I was allowed no say in it.
cues.evidence: Rückert, In diesem Wetter, first stanza as set by Mahler; German text at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindertotenlieder#Text. Our translations.

cues.title: Scoring of the fifth song
cues.text: Only this last song calls for a piccolo, a contrabassoon and a third and fourth horn. The cycle has no trumpets or trombones at all.
cues.evidence: Mahler catalogue, Kindertotenlieder, scoring list: piccolo and contrabassoon in no. 5 only, horns 3–4 in no. 5 only: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm The Mahler Foundation confirms there are no trumpets: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-introduction/

cues.title: Transition to the final stanza
cues.text: A high piccolo note and the small bell continue as the storm music slows. The string phrases fall in shorter waves. Mahler marks “Allmählich langsamer” (gradually slower) across the bridge into the final stanza.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 78–79, rehearsal 8: piccolo, Glöckchen and Allmählich langsamer; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing lullaby in D major
cues.text: The final section is marked “Langsam. Wie ein Wiegenlied” — slow, like a lullaby. Fischer-Dieskau repeats the words about the weather, now over celesta and rocking strings in D major. The children rest “als wie in der Mutter Haus” — as in their mother’s house.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 79–84: lullaby marking, two-sharp signature and Rückert’s final stanza. Our translations.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Remark to Guido Adler, 1907
cues.text: The cycle was finished in 1904. In July 1907 Mahler’s elder daughter, Maria, died of scarlet fever and diphtheria. He told Guido Adler that he had imagined “a child of mine had died”; having truly lost a daughter, he said, he “could not have written these songs any more.”
cues.evidence: Mahler to Guido Adler after Maria’s death in 1907, as quoted by Theodor Reik, The Haunting Melody (1953), p. 315, and repeated in Peter Russell, Light in Battle with Darkness: Mahler’s Kindertotenlieder (1991) and on the Mahler Foundation’s introduction: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-introduction/ (Reik and Russell seen only as full-text excerpts; the letter itself has not been traced). Maria’s death on 11 July 1907: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/the-man/health/ Kubik places the songs in the summers of 1901 and 1904: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027

cues.title: Orchestral postlude after the voice
cues.text: The baritone ends on “Haus”. The violas continue their rocking figure, and bassoon and horns play soft phrases above divided cellos.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 84–85, rehearsal 10: voice ends on Haus; rocking violas, bassoon, horns and divided cellos.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars in D major
cues.text: The celesta’s short figures descend through the last bars. Low strings, horns and clarinets hold a D major chord marked ppp, with the music marked morendo and the celesta gänzlich verklingend.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 86: Morendo dim., celesta gänzlich verklingend, final D-major chord at ppp. The existing late cue marks the closing passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cello allusion to the Third Symphony
cues.text: In the last five bars (bars 129–133) a cello melody alludes to the first theme of the Third Symphony’s finale, a movement titled “What love tells me”. The musicologist Andreas Dorschel took it as the cycle’s last word: “that death is powerful, yet love is even stronger.”
cues.evidence: Andreas Dorschel, “Trost für die Untröstlichen. Mahlers Kindertotenlieder und Bergs Violinkonzert”, Musikfreunde 25 (2012/13), no. 5, pp. 34–37 (article not opened; the allusion, mm. 129–133 of song 5, and the quoted sentence as given on the Mahler Foundation’s introduction): https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-introduction/ Kahnt full score, p. 86: the cellos’ pp morendo phrase in the last bars: https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425

transitions.title: Piccolo high D at rehearsal 8
transitions.from: A · The father in the storm
transitions.how: At rehearsal 8 the piccolo holds a high D above the orchestra as it falls back. The small bell repeats its notes over harp chords and low bassoon. At Allmählich langsamer the falling string phrases slow down, and the D minor storm music thins out.

transitions.title: D minor turns to D major
transitions.how: The piccolo holds through the change to a key signature of two sharps, and D minor becomes D major. Under the marking Langsam. Wie ein Wiegenlied, celesta and soft strings take up the rocking figure. The low strings play little around the voice when it re-enters softly.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 79, transition into the last stanza. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425

transitions.title: The violas continue after “Haus”
transitions.how: The voice ends on “Haus” and the violas carry on with their rocking figure. Divided cellos hold the bass. Horn and bassoon lines enter above, marked weich (soft). The D major postlude follows on from the lullaby without a pause.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 84, rehearsal 10, through p. 86. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song V, printed pp. 60–86: storm music, the high piccolo and small bell, then the D-major lullaby with celesta.

timeline.note: Opening storm: short wind figures, muted strings, tremolo cellos and accented harp chords.
The baritone’s line cuts across the short wind phrases and the string figures.
A held high piccolo note and the small bell remain as the storm subsides.
Celesta and soft strings accompany the lullaby; the bass line stops at its opening.
Horn and bassoon continue after the voice stops, over rocking figures in the violas and divided cellos.
The celesta descends while winds and strings play the final D-major chord.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
